title: Attraction and aversion (2.7–2.8)
hook: two sutras, almost mirror images, explain why the mind keeps chasing and keeps running
tomorrow: fear of death — even in the wise

segments.voice: Yesterday: asmita, I-ness, the seer and the mind as if fused, like glasses forgotten on your face. Did you swap I am for I notice? Today, what that I starts doing. Day four hundred fifty-one.

You walk past a bakery and smell cinnamon rolls, and before you've decided anything, you've slowed down. Your feet know. Somewhere back in your memory is a cinnamon roll that was very, very good. Then a dentist's drill starts up somewhere down the hall, and your shoulders rise. Somewhere back in your memory is a bad afternoon in a chair. Nobody chose either reaction. They were waiting. Patanjali says exactly where they were waiting.
screen: `CINNAMON ROLLS: YOU SLOW DOWN.` → `A DENTIST'S DRILL: YOU TENSE.` → `NEITHER WAS CHOSEN.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.7: sukha anushayi ragah. Attraction follows pleasure. Sutra 2.8: duhkha anushayi dveshah. Aversion follows pain. Two very short sutras, almost mirror images. The key word is anushayi, which means following after, or resting upon. Attraction rests on the memory of pleasure. Aversion rests on the memory of pain. The commentator Vyasa says it plainly: raga is the thirst for pleasure in one who remembers pleasure, and dvesha is the resentment toward pain in one who remembers pain. So these aren't random moods. They're grooves, left by experience, that pull and push the mind in advance. Now connect them to yesterday. Who got the pleasure? Who got hurt? The I, asmita. Without a me to have pleasures and pains, attraction and aversion would have nothing to hold on to. That's one reading of why they come third and fourth on the list. In these two sutras, Patanjali doesn't call pleasure itself the affliction. A cinnamon roll is a cinnamon roll. The affliction is the grip: the way a memory decides for you, before you've looked at what's actually in front of you. Attraction narrows the world to what you want. Aversion narrows it to what you're avoiding. Either way, you see less. And notice, the two are partners. A strong like often has a matching dislike close behind it: wanting the praise, dreading the criticism. Practice doesn't erase them in a day. It thins them, as sutra 2.2 promised, one noticed grip at a time.
screen: `RAGA FOLLOWS PLEASURE.` · `DVESHA FOLLOWS PAIN.` · `GROOVES LEFT BY MEMORY.` · then, large: `THE GRIP, NOT THE ROLL.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. As you sit, notice tiny pulls and pushes. An itch you want to scratch: aversion. A thought of something nice later: attraction. A sound you wish would stop. A position you'd like to shift into. Each time, name it gently, raga or dvesha, and wait one breath before doing anything. Often the pull fades by itself. If not, act, but slowly, knowing what moved you. The bell holds the time.
Attraction and aversion. Raga follows pleasure, dvesha follows pain: the third and fourth afflictions, grooves of memory that pull and push the mind.
Your line: raga, dvesha. Today, catch one craving and one avoidance as they start, and give each a single breath before you follow it. Day four hundred fifty-one.

screen: `DAY 451 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FEAR OF DEATH — EVEN IN THE WISE.`

howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers in yoga and Vedanta lineages ask students to watch raga and dvesha in daily life, pausing before acting on a like or dislike, and the Bhagavad Gita also names them as obstacles on the path.

myth: Patanjali says pleasure itself is an affliction
the affliction is raga, the grip that follows the memory of pleasure.
Vyasa ties attraction to the memory of pleasure
raga is thirst for pleasure in one who remembers pleasure.
attraction and aversion come after I-ness in the list
a me has to be there to be pleased or hurt.

fork.setup: you smell cinnamon rolls and you're already turning toward the bakery. what would 2.7 have you notice?
options: that the pull is raga, following an old memory of pleasure.
fork.reveal: attraction follows pleasure. the roll isn't the problem; the grip that decides before you look is.

original.note: Sanskrit rāga: attraction, passion; also 'color'. its mirror is dveṣa, aversion.

trapdoor: what you thought: liking and disliking are just personality.
what it means: grooves left by remembered pleasure and pain that pull and push before you choose.
what a scholar hears: anushayi ('lying after, following') ties both kleshas to memory (smriti) and to samskaras; raga also means color, which links to vairagya, 'without coloring', in 1.15.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 2.7–2.8 (attraction follows pleasure; aversion follows pain)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 2.7–2.8 (thirst for pleasure in one who remembers pleasure)
Bhagavad Gita 3.34 (attraction and aversion in the senses)

notes: Gita 3.34 reference in howItsDone (raga-dveshau in the senses' objects); confirm.

Reviewer changed 'Patanjali doesn't call pleasure bad or pain good' to 'In these two sutras, Patanjali doesn't call pleasure itself the affliction', since 2.15 says that to the discerning all is suffering (duhkham eva sarvam vivekinah). Keeper may want to nuance further.
